items.title: The day Pope Julius II laid St. Peter’s first stone
items.summary:
On Saturday, April 18, 1506, the papal court in Rome is still celebrating Easter. Pope Julius II has just had a light meal in his apartments in the Apostolic Palace, but the Resurrection of Christ isn’t the only thing on his mind. That morning, he heads for the old St. Peter’s Basilica, the church on St. Peter’s grave that is now more than 1,000 years old. He crosses the great atrium known as “Paradise,” adorned with medieval mosaics. Julius II continues on his path: the gold and enamel decorations of the courtyard and the basilica’s facade have long since lost their luster in his eyes. He barely notices Giotto’s Navicella, a mosaic depicting St. Peter’s boat. The sovereign pontiff passes through the door of the basilica, where he finds himself in a vast nave. Its dark wooden roof greatly worries his architects, especially Donato Bramante. At the far end, Bramante has erected a wall to Read More… 

The day Pope Julius II laid St. Peter’s first stone

items.title: Kraków basilica holds mass for man who committed deadly terror attack
items.summary:
On Monday, an iconic Kraków basilica held a mass for the soul of the man who killed six in the city earlier this month. 

Michał Oksiński shot six dead and injured at least 15 earlier this month just meters away from where the church is. He also killed his parents and sister before the Nov. 7 attack.

Following surprise on social media at the church’s decision, St Mary’s Basilica said the mass “in no way indicates justification for the crime” and is “an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy.”

On Sunday, a former city councillor, Łukasz Wantuch, shared online a picture of the announcement that the mass would be held Monday morning at the basilica for “the late Michał Oksiński and the deceased members of his family.”

“I won’t hide the fact that I find this somewhat shocking,” he said.

“But perhaps that is what faith is about: praying even for a murderer,” he added in a Facebook post that garnered over 1000 comments.

Later that day, the basilica shared a statement from parish administrator Father Mariusz Słonina, which said the mass “is a private initiative of one of the priests, not of St Mary’s Parish.”

However, the statement added  “praying for the deceased is an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime, a lessening of the perpetrator’s responsibility, or a trivialization of the suffering of the victims.”

According to local news service KR24, there were roughly a dozen people in attendance at the mass, with three priests presiding over the mass. 

There were uniformed police officers outside the…
items.t: Kraków basilica holds mass for man who committed deadly terror attack

items.title: Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians
items.summary:
JERUSALEM — The Vatican cardinal who oversees care of the Catholic faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem on Tuesday, saying he wanted to convey the presence of Pope Leo XIV during particularly troubled times for Christians in the region.

Cardinal Claudio Gugerotti, prefect of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Eastern Churches, prayed before the Holy Edicule inside the Church of the Holy Sepulcher, which marks the site where Christians believe Jesus was buried and rose from the dead.

“Lord, you were here physically,” Gugerotti prayed. “Lord, give hope to the world.”

Leaders of other Christian denominations in Jerusalem listened intently. The incense-filled ceremony, with clergy in solemn robes, offered a show of unity in the basilica where they have sometimes tensely shared worship space in a unique arrangement dating to the 19th century.

Preceded by bagpipers, rows of Franciscan friars and a large cross, Gugerotti and other Christian leaders processed through the narrow stone alleyways of Jerusalem’s Old City to the centuries-old church.

Harassment of clergy and faithful there has been rising. A rare violent attack on a religious sister in April sent shock waves across Israel.

“We know we are not always welcome,” said Sister Marie Reine, a Catholic nun who joined the procession in her white habit. “But our presence can bring peace, too.”

Most of Israel’s Christians are Palestinians, who have been the target of heated rhetoric after Arab-led parties made historic gains in the national elections last month. And neighboring Jordan is reeling from an attack that…
items.t: Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians

items.title: Bolivia’s ‘Andean Sistine Chapel’ gets new life as centuries-old church undergoes restoration
items.summary:
CURAHUARA DE CARANGAS, Bolivia — A 418-year-old church built and painted by Indigenous hands is getting a new lease of life in Bolivia’s high-altitude desert, where its colorful murals tell the story of an encounter between Spanish Catholicism and ancient Andean beliefs.

Known as the “Andean Sistine Chapel,” the modest adobe church in the western province of Oruro is celebrated for its elaborate murals depicting biblical scenes alongside Indigenous religious symbols.

“It is a jewel of mestizo Baroque art,” said Father Jacek Dziadosz, a Polish priest known locally as Father Jacinto. He said the church reflects how Spanish colonizers and Indigenous communities sometimes collaborated, creating a religious blend that endures today.

About a dozen Aymara workers, including several women, are putting the finishing touches on a new thatched roof and whitewashing the church’s walls ahead of the restoration’s scheduled completion in mid-December.

The project received about $66,000 from the U.S. Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation, with technical support from heritage conservation specialists and the Catholic University of Bolivia.

Finding workers skilled in traditional thatching techniques was a challenge, said Josefina Matas, a conservation specialist and university professor.

The new roof is expected to last another 25 years, withstanding freezing winds, intense sunshine, rain and hail at an altitude of around 13,100 feet, said technical supervisor Elizabeth Aguilar.

Biblical stories meet Andean beliefs

items.t: Bolivia’s ‘Andean Sistine Chapel’ gets new life as centuries-old church undergoes restoration

items.title: 400 Years of St. Peter’s Basilica!
items.summary:
The feast marked on November 18 of the dedication of the Basilicas of St. Peter and of St. Paul celebrates a history going all the way back to the Emperor Constantine, with both churches having been built under the emperor. However, in this year 2026, the feast is particularly noteworthy because the current St. Peter’s Basilica was dedicated on this day 400 years ago. While the two churches were dedicated in the early 300s, and were constructed on the sites of Peter’s and Paul’s martyrdom, the current St. Peter’s is much newer. In the early 1500s, the original church was demolished (it had lasted more than 1,000 years!) and work on the current one got underway. Then, in 1626, the present-day Basilica of Saint Peter’s at the Vatican was dedicated by Pope Urban VIII. (St. Paul’s is newer yet, with the current basilica dating back only to 1823.) Pope Leo XIV will celebrate Mass this Read More…

items.title: Married priests and women priests: The same debate?
items.summary:
Every so often, the two ideas of “married priests” and “women priests” are brought up by various people as a way to solve the priest shortage that continues to affect the United States and other parts of the Western world. The thought is that if we only allowed priests to marry, or allowed women to be ordained priests, that the priest shortage would be immediately solved. While the issue of a shortage of priests is indeed a grave one, these two proposals are actually very different. First of all, the idea of a married clergy is not something new and is in fact already an option within the greater Catholic Church. St. Peter himself was a married man, as were many of the 12 apostles. Eastern Catholics (as well as Eastern Orthodox) continue to have a tradition of allowing married men to be ordained priests. Married priests and women priests: The same debate?

items.title: What Leo gifted and received in South America
items.summary:
Papal visits produce a particular kind of diplomacy, sometimes conducted not in communiqués but in gestures, and even in objects. Over 12 days in Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru (November 6–17), Pope Leo XIV gave and received gifts that, taken together, trace the arc of his journey almost as clearly as any itinerary. On November 8, at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of the Thirty-Three in Florida, Uruguay, Leo XIV presented a Golden Rose to the image of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, patron saint of the country. The Golden Rose is one of the oldest papal distinctions, traditionally offered to shrines, churches, or cities in recognition of their devotion. In his homily, Leo said the gesture honored Mary as “the pride of our people” and asked her intercession to keep Uruguay close to Christ. items.title: Pope Leo says there is no change to agenda or priorities after his lung cancer surgery
items.summary:
ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV said his recent lung cancer surgery has not altered his agenda, outlook or even sense of mortality, as he projected a long pontificate focused on unity and healing within the church.

Leo seemed full of health, energy and jokes during an airborne news conference on Monday while returning to Rome from Peru. The grueling, 12-day trip through three South American countries left several members of the travelling Vatican delegation and press corps sick.

“I’m not 100 percent but I’m pretty good,” Leo said of his surgical recovery. “Endurance is one of the gifts the Lord gave me.”

Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 because of a cancerous tumor. He said it was discovered by chance during an annual checkup and appeared at first as a shadow on his lung.

“The first news was a surprise. There were no symptoms. I felt fine,” he said. Once the cancer was confirmed, he decided to proceed immediately to have it removed, and said he hoped his experience would help others not fear having checkups or pursue preventive care.

Leo saw no need for the provisional letter of resignation 

Prior to going into surgery, Leo said he saw no need to make provisions for the leadership of the Catholic Church if he were left medically impaired and unable to govern.

He said he hadn’t written any instructions, as his predecessors had done, outlining the criteria under which he would resign, which some legal experts believe is necessary if a pope were to end up in an irreversible coma and unable to articulate his resignation.

items.title: US Catholic bishops meet after Democrats’ big wins help reshape immigration and abortion debates
items.summary:
U.S. Catholic bishops are holding their annual fall meeting in Baltimore this week. The gathering comes just after Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories reset the political dynamics around some of the bishops’ priorities, including immigration, abortion and artificial intelligence.

The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops is now facing a divided government as it seeks to influence both the faithful and public policy.

“Midterm elections are the opportunity for people to assess where we are as a country and where we hope to go,” said Bishop Michael Burbidge of Arlington, Virginia. “I think what the citizens are asking — and we’re certainly praying for — is that those who are elected will be devoted to doing all that is right and just and true and somehow find a way to begin working together and addressing the issues that impact individuals and families.”

Catholics overall are politically mixed. Catholic voters split roughly evenly between Republican and Democratic candidates for the U.S. House, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.

There was a split between white Catholics and Latino Catholics: Just over half of white Catholics supported the Republican House candidate in their area, while about two-thirds of Latino Catholics supported the Democratic House candidate in their area.

Nationally, just over half of Catholics said the Trump administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll. A similar share disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement was doing its job.

During…
items.t: US Catholic bishops meet after Democrats’ big wins help reshape immigration and abortion debates

items.title: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
items.summary:
ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eye, saying it was merely a sign of the person’s profound faith.

Leo got hit during a popemobile ride Monday through the estimated 1.5 million people who had flooded a Lima air base for the service. Leo grimaced and touched his eye but proceeded as if nothing had happened.

During an in-flight press conference en route home, a Peruvian reporter apologized for the incident. Leo, who lived in Peru for two decades and has Peruvian citizenship, brushed it off as merely someone trying to get close to the pope.

And he also joked about it.

“The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart – or maybe in your eye – but that mark the life of someone,” he said.

“It tells you that here truly there is enthusiasm. Here there is profound faith. Here there is a desire to receive the blessing of the Lord,” he said.

People often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items toward the pope when he is in the popemobile and he has often wowed crowds with his quick reflexes and ability to catch them. His bodyguards, however, say these tossed items are some of their biggest security concerns when he’s out in public.

The post Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru appeared first on Crux .

items.title: Kindness after the horrific destruction of an image of Jesus
items.summary:
Watching a man laughing as he breaks the arm off a statue of Jesus is shocking enough. But seeing the figure fall to the pavement and shatter, while the men responsible appear to find the whole episode hilarious, feels almost physically painful. Whatever your religious beliefs, it’s difficult to understand how anyone could find such disrespect amusing, particularly when the object in question means so much to so many people. Yet this was the scene captured on CCTV in Vilnius, Lithuania, on November 11, when two men removed the corpus from a crucifix outside the Shrine of Divine Mercy. As one carried the figure away, its arms were damaged before it fell and broke into pieces. The men then fled, leaving the shattered image on the pavement. The footage has understandably prompted outrage across the world, including from people who don’t share the Catholic faith. For Catholics, the location makes the incident especially distressing. items.title: Peru gave Leo the 1st book printed in S. America, with a personal touch
items.summary:
As Pope Leo XIV concluded his visit to Peru, the country’s National Library gave him a gift that managed to be historically significant and deeply personal at once: a facsimile edition of the Doctrina Christiana y Catecismo para Instrucción de los Indios, printed in Lima in 1584 — the first book ever printed in Peru and in all of South America. The Pope signed a copy, which will be preserved in the Library’s repositories as a record of the encounter. Leo XIV left Peru on November 16, the final day of a 12-day apostolic journey through Uruguay, Argentina, and his adopted homeland. The Doctrina Christiana of 1584 is not some historical curiosity. It was a deliberate act of innovative pastoral imagination, produced under the direction of Saint Turibius of Mogrovejo, the second Archbishop of Lima, as a tool for evangelizing the indigenous populations of the Andes. Written in three languages — Spanish, Quechua, and Aymara Read More…

items.title: How St. Elizabeth of Hungary was inspired by St. Francis of Assisi
items.summary:
Interestingly some of the best-known Franciscan saints in history were individuals who possessed great wealth and power, but who eventually gave it up for the sake of the Kingdom of God. St. Francis is obviously known for selling everything he had and to give to the poor, and his life of heroic poverty inspired many others, including kings, queens, princes and princesses throughout Europe. Among the first royalty to follow in the footsteps of St. Francis in this way was St. Elizabeth of Hungary, daughter of the king of Hungary. She was sent to Germany at an early age after having been betrothed to the son of Landgrave Hermann I of Thuringia. It was in Germany where she would first encounter the Franciscan Order. items.title: Pope says he leaves Peru with what he always admired
items.summary:
“I came to proclaim Christ to you, and I leave with the witness of the faith and devotion that I always admired in you,” Pope Leo said, as he said farewell to his second homeland after an intense 12-day journey through South America. The Holy Father’s plane took off around 2:30 p.m. local time, and he has a flight home of more than 14 hours. He’s set to arrive at Rome’s Fiumicino Airport on Tuesday, November 17, at 10:25 a.m. “I have felt at home, and you have reminded me that the Church truly is a family,” Pope Leo reflected. “It was here,” he said, “that you taught me how to be a Bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter.”

items.title: Raiders fans’ incredible way to support new QB’s family

So imagine the sight at Sunday’s Las Vegas Raiders game when quarterback Fernando Mendoza scored his first NFL touchdown and a good number of supporters showed their delight sitting down. It wasn’t due to disappointment, or that the touchdown was underwhelming. The fans were wanting to honor Mendoza’s mother, Elsa, who has lived with multiple sclerosis for nearly 20 years and now uses a wheelchair. items.title: How do we face uncertainty without allowing it to overwhelm us? This Islamic teaching shows us the way
items.summary:
For generations of Muslims, tawakkul has been an essential part of faith – making a sincere effort while recognising the limits of human control

I once asked an elderly naan seller on the streets of Kabul how he was managing to make a living. It was almost midday and he had not sold a single naan. What would he take home, I asked. “Tawakkul ba Khuda,” he replied.

He had a long silver beard, deep brown eyes and a beautiful smile. As a frontline journalist covering the Afghan war, I had heard those words many times before. From a young woman trying to establish a clothing business in the middle of the conflict, to a military commander confronting a deadly insurgency, to a school student preparing for the long and uncertain journey towards a university degree, the expression seemed to surface wherever hope and hardship met.
